questions.q: Why does the lesson say training data needs governance beyond what a general data governance program already provides?
options: Machine learning models do not actually use data from an organization
Training data is never stored in any system, so no policy can apply to it
Training data is always smaller in volume than other data
Its patterns get absorbed into a model's parameters and applied to every future prediction, unlike a report that gets corrected when caught
questions.explain: The lesson's key point is that training data's influence persists in the model until retraining, unlike a report that gets corrected on the spot.

questions.q: Per the lesson, why does repurposing data for model training usually need separate sign-off?
options: Because models cannot process repurposed data at all
Because repurposed data is always technically corrupted
Because repurposing data is illegal in every jurisdiction
Because using data collected for one purpose to train a model for a different purpose is a distinct decision from its original use
questions.explain: The lesson lists 'who approved its use for this purpose' as a distinct governance question from how the data was originally collected.

questions.q: What does 'baked in' mean, as used in this lesson?
options: A model that has been permanently disconnected from the internet
Data that has been physically printed onto paper for archiving
A dataset that has been fully anonymized before any use
Training data's influence becomes embedded in a model's parameters rather than remaining a removable row in a table
questions.explain: The lesson defines 'baked in' as training data's patterns becoming compressed into the model's parameters, making removal much harder than deleting a row.

questions.q: According to the lesson, why is it harder to remove one bad data point's influence from a trained model than from a database table?
options: Because models store their training data in plain text that cannot be edited
Because the data is compressed into statistical patterns across parameters, often requiring retraining from scratch
Because deleting a row from a database is always impossible too
Because trained models are physically impossible to modify in any way
questions.explain: The lesson explains that removing a bad data point's influence from a trained model typically requires retraining, not a simple deletion.

questions.q: What does Lesson 9, referenced in this lesson's roadmap, cover?
options: How to configure cloud server firewalls
Office network security policies
The history of programming languages
How bias enters through the data itself
questions.explain: The lesson's roadmap names Lesson 9 specifically as covering bias entering through the training data.
